en: Striking the horse's ankle.
When the whip struck without warning,
For a target-shot's distance Buurul
Dragged his feet, unable to walk;
Once he had passed the target-shot's distance,
He revealed that he was a courser,
Set his feet against the ground,
And no wind could match his trot.
No livestock could match his walk.
When he ran down a slope,
His forelegs extended like a roe deer's;
When he began to climb,
His mane and tail streamed wide.
When broken, uneven ground appeared,
His feet seemed not to touch the earth;
When he began to climb,
No one could discern
Which gait the imperious courser used.
He flattened his ears like a kulan
And churned the earth like a whirlwind.
When rough and rolling ground appeared,
A flood of dust followed behind him;
The world seemed uprooted and wandering,
And your companion upon his back
Marveled whether the imperious courser
Had taken flight.
His soles clattered against the earth;
The black-steel bit
Cracked against his throat.
The places over which he passed
Were hollowed out like kilns;
Where his sliding hoof struck,
The earth was cut into embankments.
The ground crumbled beneath his steps,
And clods as large as a house
Shrieked above the head
Of the young man whose road lay hard.
Steam issuing from his nostrils
Billowed like the smoke of an army.
Stones struck squarely by his hooves
Split apart with ringing cracks,
And shattered with shrill cries.
Lengthening his stride like an argali,
Ah, that creature, the horse Buurul,
Reddened at the eyes like a ram,
Flung his forelock toward the sky,
Hammered his hooves into the earth,
And the ground wheeled in the mirage,
Drawing near the place he must reach,
The companion upon his back,
From running so hard,
Felt his senses reel and scatter.
His tail, fine as willow silk,
Separated into strand after strand
And streamed behind him.
When visible, Buurul shuddered and flashed;
When unseen, he billowed like blue smoke.
His mouth gaped wide as a cavern;
As one watched the courser,
White foam mingled with blood
Scattered across his chest.
When he ran down a slope,
That creature unlike other beasts
Raced with flying birds.
His four basin-wide hooves,
Once his flesh grew hot,
Struck against one another.
Kulchoro upon his back
Wrestled with the mouth
Of Buurul standing in the line.
His hands cramped upon the white reins knotted in loops;
He could not pull them back.
This poor beast was truly born of the unseen
And had broken into an open run:
"Will he go racing headlong?
If broken, hollow ground appears,
Will my death come needlessly?
Is this how my fate will end?
I have never seen," said Kulchoro,
"A kinsman like Semetey!"
He traveled on unable to rein the mouth
Of the courser restored to fighting condition.
His eyes rolled wildly,
And his legs dangled loose;
Struggling against the horse's mouth,
Kulchoro traveled on
Clinging to Akkangky.
Struggling for his life,
Kulchoro grappled fiercely
With renowned Buurul.
Tall Buurul carried him away
Into the hollow of Ak-Kyya,
Then wheeled, descended, and stopped
Beside Great Urgench.
Looking, the eye could seize nothing;
The mist-shrouded companion
Could not tell what lay before him.
For as long as it takes tea to boil,
Like a person overcome with exhaustion,
He could not open his streaming eyes,
Nor properly settle his heart.
As he stood there dumbfounded,
The high mountains thundered;
When Choro stopped and looked,
The birches and poplars
Roared as though a wind were blowing.
It pounded until the ear went deaf,
Gathering and rushing with a roar.
Its name was the River Urgench,
And its surface was foam and vapor.
Overturning and pouring onward,
When he looked downstream,
It appeared like four rivers.
It thundered in humps like a camel's back,
The free body of your lordly companion
Shuddered and trembled through its length.
The mud rolled like a gray turban;
Heroic Kulchoro
Drew back, invoking God.
When he looked at Great Urgench,
It was filled with spectacle.
It surged and thundered in billows;
Its middle ran violently fast,
All its waters flowing together without circling,
Flowing far greater than a sea.
Its center rushed beyond all measure,
And avalanche snow flowed at its edges.
The sight opened the heart;
It appeared like a lake and river together.
If you would see a wonder, see it here:
Young firs and pines
Were torn out by their roots,
Struck against the bank,
And stripped the cliffside bare.
Watching it, Kulchoro
Felt his whole age shrivel.
Every gully and slope was flushed red;
Crosscurrents strong enough to sweep away horses
Spurted from every place,
Joining in a thousand channels.
Pines and rafts swept along,
And birches and willows floated;
They gathered into a flood
And struck against every bank.
The companion watching it cried,
"May God preserve me!"
Far from being able to cross it then,
His whole age shriveled.
Foam fluttered upon its surface;
House-sized stones from its bed
All rolled onward with a clatter.
It gathered force like the cuckoo's call;
Great Urgench rushed and roared,
Taking on countless different forms.
The earth split and cliffs collapsed,
And all the water turned to mud.
Kulchoro, watching,
Clutched his collar and invoked God.
A gray roll of mud as large as a house
Fell in and churned away;
Kulchoro watched closely,
And his whole age shriveled.
If he cast a bridle into the rebounding foam
That flowed along its edge, it could not touch bottom;
Even a swift fox could not range across it.
Kulchoro did not think,
"I shall reach the farther bank."
If he cast a rope into the foam
Kicked upward by the torrent, it could not touch bottom;
Even a fox could not range its high banks.
From the force of Urgench
A roaring windstorm blew.
Birches and willows, roots and all,
Swept past in a thundering mass.
A person saying, "I shall cross"—
It would reach up to his kidneys
If this flood struck him,
It would tear him limb from limb.
All the glaciers had broken apart
And poured down in an altered flood.
Spreading wide, flowing, and spilling,
When one looked at Great Urgench,
To the companion standing there
It appeared like a devouring beast.
Urgench had entered flood like this
Because your discerning sister-in-law Churok,
That troublesome poor woman,
Knew that her lord would come.
"If that gray wolf is a hero,
Let him ride forward and cross the water;
If he is a coward, let him falter
And flee back the way he came,"
Of poor Kozho and Toltoy—
If Semetey possesses their courage,
Let him pursue the matter to its end;
If Semetey lacks courage,
Let him turn back
From this flowing river."
Pondering every kind of scheme,
To test his heroism
And take her vengeance
Still unspent upon Chynkojo and Toltoy,
She read words in Arabic
And cast a spell upon the weather.
All the glaciers broke apart,
And springs overflowed and streamed;
Hail fell across all the uplands,
And rain across the riverlands;
Every slope ran red,
And pale water flowing from the heights
Joined from every direction.
It flowed black and filthy,
Filling the gorge as one body.
Because of Churok,
It ran muddy and stinking of dung,
Entering a flood no one could withstand.
Those who saw it invoked God;
Its foam heaved and divided,
And to the companion watching
It appeared like a devouring beast.
Kulchoro, who had never seen such water,
Grieved at the sight of it.
When he saw Great Urgench,
The poor hero stood in terror,
Despairing of his borrowed life:
"Does one who crosses this Urgench
Not die in terrible distress,
And behold the face of Judgment Day?
Does one who crosses ever turn back?
Does one who meets it return alive?
It is water like a devouring beast.
I shall return to my elder Semetey
And tell my elder
That its waters are too fierce."
Kulchoro wheeled about
And now turned Buurul's head;
He turned and stood examining
The land and water of this Urgench.
Ah, that creature, Great Urgench:
Its leaves were broad as leather,
Its black beetles thick as thumbs,
Its lizards like snakes,
And its snakes like ropes seven fathoms long.
Almighty God in his power
Creates living souls of every kind.
Its saplings were like plane trees,
Its small birds like snowcocks,
And its hogweed stalks thick as forearms;
When you looked at its red deer,
They were like pale, white-faced cows.
It was a broad and tranquil land,
Its apples ripening until they became compost,
A place of wonders of every kind.
Kulchoro stood astonished;
When he looked toward the farther bank,
